questions.q: What is the standard formula defining cardiac output (CO) and its normal resting value in a healthy 70 kg adult male?
options: CO = Stroke Volume x Heart Rate; approximately 5.0 to 5.5 L/min
CO = End-Diastolic Volume x Heart Rate; approximately 9.0 L/min
CO = Mean Arterial Pressure x Total Peripheral Resistance; approximately 500 mL/min
CO = Stroke Volume / Heart Rate; approximately 1.0 L/min
questions.explain: Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute (CO = SV x HR). At a resting stroke volume of ~70 mL and heart rate of ~72 bpm, resting CO averages ~5.0 to 5.5 L/min.

open.q: State the mathematical formula for cardiac output and give its normal resting value in liters per minute for a healthy 70 kg adult male.
accept: CO = Stroke volume x Heart rate; 5 to 5.5 L/min
Stroke volume multiplied by heart rate; ~5 L/min

questions.q: What is the cardiac index (CI), and what is its normal resting value in healthy adults?
options: Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume; normally 60%
Cardiac output divided by total body surface area (BSA); normally 3.0 to 3.4 L/min/m2
Heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure; normally 0.6
Cardiac output multiplied by body weight in kilograms; normally 350 L/min
questions.explain: Because resting cardiac output varies directly with body size, normalizing CO to body surface area (average BSA ~1.7 m2) yields the cardiac index (CI = CO / BSA), normally ~3.0 to 3.4 L/min/m2.

open.q: Define cardiac index and state its normal resting reference value in healthy adults.
accept: Cardiac output divided by body surface area; 3.0 to 3.4 L/min/m2
CO / BSA; approximately 3.2 L/min/m2

questions.q: What is cardiac reserve, and roughly how much can cardiac output increase in a healthy untrained young adult versus a trained endurance athlete during maximal exercise?
options: The difference between right and left ventricular output
Residual volume remaining after systole
The ability to raise cardiac output above rest; peak output is higher in trained athletes
The volume of blood stored in the spleen
questions.explain: Cardiac reserve is the capacity to elevate CO above resting baseline (Maximum CO minus Resting CO, or expressed as a percentage). Untrained adults reach ~20-25 L/min (~300-400% reserve), while elite marathon runners can exceed 30-35 L/min.

open.q: Define cardiac reserve and give the approximate maximal cardiac output achievable during strenuous exercise in an untrained adult versus a trained endurance athlete.
accept: Maximum CO minus resting CO; ~20-25 L/min in untrained adults and ~30-35 L/min in trained athletes
Percentage increase in CO above rest; 300-400% untrained vs 500-600% athlete

questions.q: Which equation expresses the direct Fick principle for measuring cardiac output?
options: CO = (Arterial O2 content - Venous O2 content) / Whole-body O2 consumption
CO = Whole-body O2 consumption x (Arterial O2 content - Mixed venous O2 content)
CO = Mixed venous O2 content / Arterial O2 content
CO = Whole-body O2 consumption (VO2) / (Arterial O2 content - Mixed venous O2 content)
questions.explain: By conservation of mass across the pulmonary capillaries, O2 uptake by lungs (VO2) equals blood flow (CO) multiplied by the arteriovenous O2 content difference (CaO2 - CvO2); rearranging gives CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2).

open.q: Write the Fick principle formula used to calculate cardiac output from oxygen consumption and blood oxygen contents.
accept: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2)
Cardiac output = Oxygen consumption / (Arterial O2 content - Mixed venous O2 content)

questions.q: In a Fick principle determination, a patient has an oxygen consumption (VO2) of 250 mL/min, a systemic arterial O2 content of 200 mL O2/L blood, and a pulmonary artery mixed venous O2 content of 150 mL O2/L blood. What is the cardiac output?
options: 5.0 L/min
2.5 L/min
12.5 L/min
1.25 L/min

open.q: Calculate cardiac output if oxygen consumption is 250 mL/min, arterial oxygen content is 200 mL/L, and mixed venous oxygen content is 150 mL/L.
accept: 5 L/min
5.0 liters per minute
5000 mL/min

questions.q: From which anatomical site must a blood sample be drawn to obtain true mixed venous oxygen content (CvO2) for the Fick cardiac output calculation?
options: Antecubital vein
Pulmonary artery (via a Swan-Ganz catheter)
Inferior vena cava
Coronary sinus
questions.explain: Different organs extract varying amounts of O2 (for example, myocardium extracts ~65% whereas kidneys extract ~10%), so venous blood from the SVC, IVC, and coronary sinus does not fully mix until reaching the right ventricle and pulmonary artery.

open.q: From which blood vessel must blood be sampled to measure true mixed venous oxygen content in the direct Fick method?
accept: Pulmonary artery
Main pulmonary artery

questions.q: In the thermodilution (Stewart-Hamilton indicator dilution) technique using a pulmonary artery catheter, how does the area under the downstream temperature-time curve relate to cardiac output?
options: Cardiac output is directly proportional to the area under the curve
Cardiac output is independent of the area under the curve
Cardiac output is inversely proportional to the area under the curve
Cardiac output equals the square of the peak temperature drop
questions.explain: When cold saline is injected into the right atrium, rapid blood flow washes the cold bolus past the pulmonary artery thermistor quickly, producing a small area under the curve; slow blood flow produces a broad curve with a large area (CO = Indicator dose / Area under curve).

open.q: In indicator-dilution and thermodilution measurements of cardiac output, how is cardiac output mathematically related to the area under the primary concentration-time or temperature-time curve?
accept: Inversely proportional to the area under the curve
CO equals amount of indicator divided by area under the curve

questions.q: Which three primary physiological determinants govern ventricular stroke volume?
options: Heart rate, blood viscosity, and plasma osmolarity
Coronary blood flow, bronchial tone, and glomerular filtration rate
Carotid sinus firing, jugular venous pressure, and hematocrit
Preload, myocardial contractility (inotropy), and afterload
questions.explain: Stroke volume is determined by preload (end-diastolic sarcomere stretch/EDV), intrinsic myocardial contractility (force generated at a given preload), and afterload (arterial impedance opposing ejection).

open.q: Name the three principal physiological factors that determine ventricular stroke volume.
accept: Preload, contractility, and afterload
Preload, inotropy, and afterload

questions.q: How does homeometric autoregulation (the Anrep effect) differ from heterometric autoregulation (the Frank-Starling mechanism)?
options: Anrep increases contractility at fixed fibre length; Frank–Starling increases force through greater end-diastolic stretch
Anrep slows heart rate during inspiration; Frank–Starling raises it during expiration
Anrep depends on vagal acetylcholine; Frank–Starling depends on aldosterone
Anrep occurs only in skeletal muscle; Frank–Starling only in smooth muscle
questions.explain: Heterometric regulation adjusts force through changes in initial sarcomere length (EDV); homeometric regulation (Anrep effect and Bowditch staircase/Treppe phenomenon) enhances contractility independently of fiber length by increasing intracellular Ca2+ availability.

open.q: Contrast heterometric autoregulation (Frank-Starling mechanism) with homeometric autoregulation (Anrep effect) in cardiac muscle.
accept: Heterometric depends on changes in end-diastolic fiber length, whereas homeometric increases contractility without changing resting fiber length
Frank-Starling acts via increased preload/length; Anrep increases contractility at constant fiber length after raised afterload

questions.q: What is the Bowditch effect (treppe or force-frequency relationship) in ventricular myocardium?
options: A progressive fall in stroke volume when venous return rises
Contractile force increases with heart rate, partly through greater intracellular Ca2+ availability
Cardiac arrest triggered by carotid sinus massage
Reflex vasodilation of skeletal muscle arterioles during sleep
questions.explain: Higher heart rates produce more action potentials per minute, increasing total L-type Ca2+ influx and outpacing NCX extrusion so sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ stores build up and strengthen contraction.

open.q: Explain the physiological mechanism behind the Bowditch (treppe or staircase) phenomenon when heart rate increases.
accept: Increased frequency of depolarization causes cumulative intracellular Ca2+ accumulation in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, boosting contractility
More frequent Ca2+ influx per minute increases SR Ca2+ stores and contractile force

questions.sub: Venous Return and Guyton Vascular Function Curves
questions.q: According to Guyton's hemodynamic equation for venous return (VR), which formula defines venous return?
options: VR = Right atrial pressure / Mean systemic filling pressure
VR = Mean arterial pressure x Venous compliance
VR = (Mean systemic filling pressure - Right atrial pressure) / Resistance to venous return
VR = Stroke volume x Right atrial pressure
questions.explain: Blood flows back to the right atrium down the pressure gradient between the mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf, ~7 mmHg) and right atrial pressure (Pra, ~0-2 mmHg), divided by resistance to venous return (Rvr).

open.q: Write Guyton's equation relating venous return (VR) to mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf), right atrial pressure (Pra), and resistance to venous return (Rvr).
accept: VR = (Pmsf - Pra) / Rvr
Venous return = (Mean systemic filling pressure - Right atrial pressure) / Resistance to venous return

questions.sub: Venous Return and Guyton Vascular Function Curves
questions.q: What is the mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf), and what is its normal value in a healthy resting adult?
options: Peak aortic systolic pressure, normally 120 mmHg
Capillary hydrostatic pressure, normally 35 mmHg
Pulmonary artery wedge pressure, normally 25 mmHg
The pressure after circulatory pressures equilibrate when the heart stops, normally about 7 mmHg
questions.explain: Pmsf (~7 mmHg) reflects the degree of filling (stressed blood volume) relative to systemic vascular compliance; it rises with blood transfusion or sympathetic venoconstriction and falls with hemorrhage.

open.q: Define mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf) and state its normal value in mmHg.
accept: Equilibrium pressure throughout the systemic circulation when the heart is stopped; ~7 mmHg
Static pressure in systemic vessels at zero flow; about 7 mmHg

questions.sub: Venous Return and Guyton Vascular Function Curves
questions.q: On Guyton's venous return (vascular function) curve, why does venous return reach a flat plateau when right atrial pressure drops below 0 mmHg?
options: Great veins entering the thorax collapse when intraluminal pressure becomes sufficiently negative
The tricuspid valve locks shut below zero right atrial pressure
Skeletal muscle pumps stop contracting at negative right atrial pressure
The SA node stops firing when right atrial pressure falls below zero
questions.explain: Because thin-walled extrathoracic veins (such as the venae cavae entering the chest) are collapsible, suction below ~0 mmHg collapses the vessel wall and prevents any further increase in venous return.

open.q: Why does venous return fail to increase further when right atrial pressure falls lower than 0 mmHg?
accept: Collapse of the great veins entering the thorax
Collapsible venae cavae pinch shut when intraluminal pressure becomes negative

questions.sub: Venous Return and Guyton Vascular Function Curves
questions.q: How do acute blood volume expansion (transfusion) and sympathetic venoconstriction shift the Guyton venous return curve?
options: They lower mean systemic filling pressure and shift the curve down and left
They raise mean systemic filling pressure, shifting the venous-return curve up and right
They change only the cardiac function curve
They collapse pulmonary veins and reduce left atrial pressure to zero
questions.explain: Both increased blood volume and alpha-1-mediated constriction of compliant venous capacitance reservoirs raise Pmsf, shifting the vascular function curve right/upward and intersecting the cardiac curve at higher right atrial pressure and higher cardiac output.

open.q: How do blood transfusion and sympathetic venoconstriction affect mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf) and the position of the venous return curve?
accept: They increase Pmsf and shift the venous return curve upward and to the right
Raise mean systemic filling pressure and shift the vascular function curve rightward

questions.sub: Venous Return and Guyton Vascular Function Curves
questions.q: In an arteriovenous (AV) fistula, blood bypasses high-resistance arterioles and flows directly from an artery into a vein. How does this alter resistance to venous return and steady-state cardiac output?
options: Increases resistance to venous return and lowers cardiac output
Has no effect on venous return or cardiac output
Decreases resistance to venous return, rotating the venous return curve clockwise upward and markedly increasing cardiac output
Lowers heart rate to 30 beats/min via the Bainbridge reflex
questions.explain: Shunting blood directly from artery to vein dramatically drops total peripheral resistance and resistance to venous return (Rvr), increasing the upward slope of the venous return curve and producing high-output cardiac states.

open.q: How does a large arteriovenous (AV) shunt affect resistance to venous return and steady-state cardiac output?
accept: Decreases resistance to venous return and increases cardiac output
Lowers Rvr, steepens the venous return curve, and elevates CO

questions.q: Which four physiological mechanisms assist venous return from the lower extremities and abdomen back to the right atrium against gravity?
options: Arteriolar constriction, lymphatic blockade, bronchoconstriction, and Valsalva maneuver
Mitral valve closure, carotid sinus baroreflex, renal natriuresis, and sweating
Aortic elastic recoil, coronary sinus flow, cerebrospinal fluid absorption, and peristalsis
Skeletal muscle pump with one-way venous valves, respiratory (abdominothoracic) pump, sympathetic venoconstriction, and cardiac suction
questions.explain: Rhythmic calf muscle contraction compresses deep veins past bicuspid valves (muscle pump); inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure while raising intra-abdominal pressure (respiratory pump); sympathetic tone mobilizes unstressed venous blood; and downward displacement of the AV valve ring during ventricular ejection draws blood into the atria.

open.q: List three physiological mechanisms that promote venous return from the lower body to the heart.
accept: Skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pump, and sympathetic venoconstriction
Venous valves with muscle pump, thoracic respiratory pump, and cardiac suction

questions.sub: Regulation of Heart Rate and Bainbridge Reflex
questions.q: What is the Bainbridge (atrial) reflex?
options: Reflex tachycardia triggered by stretch of atrial volume receptors when venous return and right atrial pressure rise acutely
Reflex bradycardia triggered by high pressure in the carotid sinus
Apnea and bradycardia triggered by cold water on the face
Coronary vasodilation triggered by myocardial adenosine release
questions.explain: Rapid intravenous infusion stretches low-pressure type B atrial mechanoreceptors, sending vagal afferents to the medulla to increase sympathetic outflow to the SA node (preventing blood damming in the veins and atria).

open.q: Describe the stimulus and cardiovascular response of the Bainbridge reflex.
accept: Increased right atrial filling/stretch causes reflex tachycardia to prevent venous congestion
Atrial volume receptor stretch triggers an increase in heart rate

questions.sub: Regulation of Heart Rate and Bainbridge Reflex
questions.q: Why does cardiac output fall precipitously if ventricular heart rate rises excessively above 180 to 200 beats per minute (such as in severe supraventricular tachycardia)?
options: Myocardial actin and myosin denature above 180 beats/min
Shortened diastolic filling reduces end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
The aortic valve cannot open more than 150 times per minute
Vagal tone overrides sympathetic stimulation at high heart rates
questions.explain: Because tachycardia encroaches primarily on diastole, extreme heart rates shorten ventricular filling time severely, reducing preload and stroke volume so markedly that CO = HR x SV declines.

open.q: Why does extreme tachycardia (higher than ~180-200 beats/min) reduce rather than increase cardiac output?
accept: Diastolic filling time becomes too short, markedly reducing end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
Shortened diastole impairs ventricular filling and lowers stroke volume

questions.q: What happens to cardiac output when a person moves rapidly from a supine (lying) position to an upright standing position?
options: Cardiac output rises by 40% because standing increases venous return
Cardiac output remains completely unchanged
Venous pooling reduces preload and stroke volume, so cardiac output initially falls
Cardiac output doubles because the respiratory pump becomes more effective
questions.explain: Standing pools roughly 500 mL of blood in compliant lower-extremity veins, decreasing venous return, EDV, and stroke volume by ~30-40%; baroreceptor-mediated reflex tachycardia partially compensates, leaving net CO ~20% lower than supine.

open.q: How and why does cardiac output change when transitioning from lying supine to standing upright?
accept: Decreases by about 20% due to gravitational venous pooling in the legs lowering venous return and stroke volume
CO falls (~20%) because venous pooling reduces preload

questions.q: Which physiological state increases resting cardiac output by 30% to 50%, peaking around the end of the second to early third trimester?
options: Deep non-REM sleep
Hypothyroidism
Acute hemorrhage
Normal pregnancy
questions.explain: During pregnancy, blood volume expansion, low-resistance uteroplacental circulation, and elevated metabolic demand boost cardiac output by 30-50% above non-pregnant baseline.

open.q: By approximately what percentage does maternal cardiac output increase during normal pregnancy?
accept: About 40%

questions.q: During dynamic isotonic exercise (such as running), how do heart rate, stroke volume, and total peripheral resistance change to elevate cardiac output up to 4- or 5-fold?
options: Heart rate and stroke volume rise while metabolic vasodilation lowers total peripheral resistance
Heart rate stays constant while stroke volume increases fivefold
Total peripheral resistance doubles while stroke volume halves
Venous return falls and myocardial contractility decreases
questions.explain: In dynamic exercise, sympathetic activation and vagal withdrawal raise HR (up to ~180-200 bpm) and contractility, muscle/respiratory pumps boost venous return and SV, and local metabolites (adenosine, K+, H+, NO) dilate muscle arterioles to lower TPR.

open.q: Summarize the changes in heart rate, stroke volume, and total peripheral resistance that enable a large rise in cardiac output during dynamic aerobic exercise.
accept: Heart rate rises sharply, stroke volume increases moderately, and total peripheral resistance decreases
Increased HR and SV combined with reduced TPR

questions.q: Which group of clinical conditions produces a 'high-output' state characterized by chronically elevated resting cardiac output alongside reduced systemic vascular resistance?
options: Myocardial infarction, tamponade and severe hypothyroidism
Severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, beriberi and arteriovenous fistula
Haemorrhagic shock, aortic stenosis and restrictive cardiomyopathy
Complete heart block, pulmonary embolism and dehydration
questions.explain: High-output states occur when reduced blood viscosity/tissue hypoxia (severe anemia), systemic vasodilation/hypermetabolism (thyrotoxicosis, wet beriberi), or direct vascular shunting (AV fistula, Paget bone disease) lower TPR and boost venous return.

open.q: Name three pathological conditions that cause a high-output cardiac state.
accept: Severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, and beriberi
Anemia, hyperthyroidism, and arteriovenous fistula

questions.q: A 42-year-old man involved in a high-speed road traffic accident presents with hypotension (BP 78/50 mmHg), tachycardia (132 bpm), distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). Echocardiography confirms acute pericardial tamponade. What is the direct hemodynamic mechanism reducing his cardiac output?
options: Loss of SA-node automaticity is the primary cause of reduced output
Systemic arteriolar vasodilation is the main mechanism
Pericardial pressure restricts diastolic filling, reducing preload and stroke volume
Descending aortic obstruction prevents ventricular ejection
questions.explain: In cardiac tamponade, fluid trapped inside the non-compliant pericardial sac compresses all cardiac chambers, preventing normal diastolic filling (impaired preload) so stroke volume and cardiac output fall precipitously despite high venous pressure.

open.q: Explain how acute cardiac tamponade causes a rapid drop in cardiac output.
accept: Intrapericardial pressure compresses the heart and prevents ventricular diastolic filling, reducing preload and stroke volume
Restricted diastolic expansion severely lowers ventricular preload and stroke volume

questions.q: A 65-year-old man with decompensated left ventricular systolic heart failure receives an intravenous infusion of dobutamine (a beta-1 adrenergic agonist) and a venodilator. On Guyton's cardiac and vascular function curves, how does dobutamine alone shift the cardiac function curve?
options: Downward and rightward, reducing output at every right atrial pressure
It shifts only the venous-return curve
It eliminates the plateau of the cardiac function curve
It shifts the cardiac function curve upward and leftward, increasing output at a given right atrial pressure
questions.explain: Positive inotropic stimulation shifts the cardiac output curve upward/leftward; intersecting the unchanged venous return curve yields a higher steady-state cardiac output and lower right atrial pressure (relieving venous congestion).

open.q: How does a positive inotropic agent shift Guyton's cardiac output curve, and what happens to steady-state cardiac output and right atrial pressure?
accept: Shifts the cardiac function curve upward and leftward, increasing cardiac output and lowering right atrial pressure
Upward shift of cardiac curve leading to higher CO and lower Pra

questions.q: Which non-invasive bedside imaging method measures cardiac output by combining the cross-sectional area of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) with the velocity-time integral (VTI) of blood flow across the aortic valve?
options: Doppler echocardiography
Chest radiography
Standard 12-lead surface ECG
Pulse oximetry
questions.explain: Doppler echocardiography calculates stroke volume as LVOT area x LVOT VTI (velocity-time integral) and multiplies by heart rate to estimate cardiac output non-invasively without vascular catheterization.

open.q: Name the non-invasive ultrasound technique used clinically to measure stroke volume and cardiac output across the left ventricular outflow tract.
accept: Doppler echocardiography
Echocardiography
Transthoracic Doppler echo
